questions.topic: while vs for: similarity and difference
questions.question: State one similarity and one difference between while and for loop.
questions.solution:
Similarity: both are entry-controlled loops; the condition is tested before the body runs, and the body repeats while the condition is true.
Difference: a for loop is used when the number of iterations is known in advance (initialisation, condition and update are written in one line); a while loop is used when the number of iterations is not known and depends on a condition (e.g. user input).

questions.question: Compare all the three types of loops?
questions.solution:
for loop: used when the number of iterations is known in advance; entry-controlled (condition checked before the body).
while loop: used when the number of iterations is not known beforehand; entry-controlled, so the body may not run even once.
do-while loop: used when the body must run at least once (e.g. a menu that asks whether to repeat); exit-controlled, the condition is checked after the body.

marking_points.point: Usage of for vs while (known vs unknown iterations)
do-while is exit-controlled / runs at least once; for and while are entry-controlled

questions.question: What is the difference between break and labelled break?
questions.solution:
An unlabelled break terminates only the innermost loop (or switch) in which it appears.
A labelled break (break label;) terminates the loop marked with that label, so it can end an outer loop from inside an inner loop.
Example:
outer:
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
    for (int j = 1; j <= 3; j++)
        if (j == 2) break outer;  // ends both loops

marking_points.point: labelled break ends the labelled (outer) loop

questions.question:
Assertion (A) : Wrapper classes in Java are used to treat primitive types as objects.
Reason (R) : Wrapper classes enable the use of primitive data types in data structures like ArrayList and HashMap.

options.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.b: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.c: A is true, but R is false.
options.d: A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution: (a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Structures such as ArrayList and HashMap store only objects, so a primitive must be wrapped (e.g. int as Integer) to be stored; that is why wrapper classes exist.

questions.question: On what basis are the classes grouped?
questions.solution: Java's library classes are grouped into packages according to the functions they perform: classes doing related work are put in the same package. For example, java.lang holds the basic language classes (String, Math, wrapper classes), java.util holds utility classes (Scanner), and java.io holds input/output classes. (Corrected: the source key described a class grouping similar objects; in this chapter the question is about grouping classes into packages.)

marking_points.point: Grouping is by related function, with an example

questions.question: What are library classes? Give an example.
questions.solution:
Library classes are the pre-defined (built-in) classes supplied with Java, grouped into packages, which a program can use directly without writing them. They have their own data members, constructors and methods.
Examples: Math, String, Scanner, Integer, Character.

questions.topic: Library classes are grouped in packages
questions.question: Where are these classes (the library classes of Java) grouped together and placed?

answer_items.prompt: Library classes are grouped together in

questions.solution: In packages. Related library classes are grouped together in packages, which together form the Java class library.

questions.question: Write the benefit of grouping the classes as packages?
questions.solution:
(i) Easier management: thousands of classes are organised by function, so a needed class is easy to find and import.
(ii) Visibility control and no name clashes: access to classes and members can be restricted to the package, and two classes with the same name can exist in different packages.
(Also: reusability, since classes in a package can be used in any program by importing them.)

marking_points.point: A second benefit (access control / avoiding name clashes / reusability)

questions.question: What are the two categories of packages?
questions.solution:
(i) Built-in (Java API) packages, e.g. java.lang, java.util, java.io.
(ii) User-defined packages, created by the programmer with the package keyword.

questions.question: What is meant by a package? Name any two Java Application Programming Interface packages.

A package is a group (namespace, like a folder) of related classes and interfaces.
Two Java API packages: java.lang and java.util (others: java.io, java.math).

questions.question: What are Java API packages?
questions.solution: Java API (Application Programming Interface) packages are the built-in packages supplied with Java, in which the library classes are grouped according to their function, e.g. java.lang, java.util, java.io. Their classes can be imported into a program as needed.
